transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
A vote in the House is expected this week on articles of impeachment against Defense
Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The effort is being led by an outgoing Republican congressman, as NPR's Barbara Sprunk reports.
Congressman Thomas Massey has long been a critic of Secretary Hegseth.
The Kentucky Republican first tried to bring an impeachment resolution ahead of the midterm
elections, but House Speaker Mike Johnson called an early recess to avoid the vote.
Massey's impeachment resolution lists eight charges against Hegseth, including illegally
waging war against Iran, overseeing extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean, and suppressing
free speech.
The argument here is that he's broken laws and he's violated the Constitution.
There will likely be sufficient votes in the House to impeach, but it's unlikely to clear
the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office, which requires
two-thirds of the Senate.
Barbara Sprunk and PR News, Washington.
Wall Street is coming off the day of sharp gains.
The Dow and the S&P each gained more than 2 percent yesterday.
The Nasdaq finished the trading session up nearly two and three-quarters percent.
Analysts say investors were in a buying mood after last week's sharp sell-off.
Researchers of computer giant Nvidia lost more than 4 percent after the company reported
it was investigating its CEO and co-founder over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
NPR's Scott Horsley says new numbers on inflation in the U.S. economy are due out today from
the Labor Department.
A year ago, hundreds of government price checkers were idled by a six-week federal shutdown,
so prices from October of 2025 were never officially collected.
As a result, the Labor Department won't be issuing its usual report on how the cost of
living has risen over the last 12 months.
It will report on how costs have increased between September and October of this year.
Falling gas prices have given drivers some relief in recent weeks, but diesel prices
have come down only slowly.
The Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank estimates that prices overall have risen about 3.7 percent
in the last year.
That means prices are climbing faster than average wages, so the typical worker is losing
buying power.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Voters in California have rejected a wealth tax, as Laura Fitzgerald with Member Station
KQED reports.
California's Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time, 5 percent wealth tax on the state's
billionaires.
Around 53 percent of voters opposed it.
Prop 40 was backed by a health care workers union, and most of the revenue would have
been used to fund health care.
Opponents, including Governor Gavin Newsom, said the tax would ultimately hurt the state's
budget.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin funneled over $100 million into two measures designed to
cancel out the wealth tax.
For NPR News, I'm Laura Fitzgerald in San Francisco.
Wall Street futures are higher this morning.
This is NPR News.
Negotiations to try to end Russia's war with Ukraine are underway in the United Arab Emirates.
Two days of talks began earlier today in Abu Dhabi, involving officials from Moscow, Kiev,
and the U.S.
President Trump's special envoy, Steve Whitcoff, and the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner,
are leading the U.S. delegation.
Security guarantees are expected to be one of the main issues.
U.N. climate talks are underway in Turkey.
U.S. officials are not attending the annual COP 31 summit, but some governors and environmental
groups are, as NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchi reports from Antalya.
A coalition of major U.S. climate groups announced that more than 120 governors, mayors and local
leaders will attend the COP 31 summit.
In a statement, the group said it wants to show that the U.S. remains committed to emission
reductions in clean energy investments, regardless of federal policy changes.
The Trump administration has phased out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind systems,
reduced regulations for greenhouse gases, and ended renewable energy projects.
The coalition, led by New Mexico governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, said it will be at
the summit to launch new research on how the U.S. can slash its emissions.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Antalya.
The Food and Drug Administration is adding a new warning to GLP-1 drugs used by millions
of people for weight loss and to treat diabetes.
The FDA says vision loss is possible, though rare.
The new language warns doctors about the eye condition which the FDA says can be permanent.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from Cure Alzheimer's Fund.
From family to community, connections and the memories they make are everything.
The hugs, the strolls, the laughs, songs and dreams.
Cure Alzheimer's Fund empowers the scientists who dedicate their lives to curing Alzheimer's
disease.
Great progress has been made and the momentum is building.
There is more to do.
Learn more at curealz.org.
Let's keep our memories together.

topics.text: Vote expected in House on impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Wall Street rallies sharply after last week's sell-off; Nvidia shares fall over CEO affair report
Labor Department to release inflation figures covering September to October 2025 prices
California voters reject Proposition 40, a one-time wealth tax on billionaires
US-Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations begin in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
US climate groups and governors attend U.N. COP 31 climate summit in Turkey
FDA adds warning about rare, possibly permanent vision loss to GLP-1 drugs
